title: Ayoyo Soup
author: Steyn Hoogakker
desc: Wash the leaves before cutting, otherwise the sliminess will not be activated — the one instruction that decides whether ayoyo works.
longDesc: Ayoyo is jute leaf and the soup is wanted for its slipperiness. The single most important instruction in the documented record is here: wash the ayoyo leaves before cutting, otherwise the sliminess will not be activated. A hundred and fifty grams of leaves, fifteen grams of dawadawa, a calabash nut and fifty grams of dried local herring are the northern seasoning core. Onion, dawadawa, calabash nut and herring are blended, a cup of boiling water goes in, then five minutes' wait before the leaves, and about ten minutes' simmer — blended or stirred with an ijabe broom.
ingredients: 250 g beef chunks, or 200 g fresh salmon or mushrooms
1 seasoning cube dissolved in 250 ml water, or 250 ml meat stock
// For the tuo, if making the full dish
1.5 litres water — see the note on this figure
steps: Wash the ayoyo leaves BEFORE cutting them, otherwise the sliminess will not be activated.
Cook the stew base — onion, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, pepper, palm oil and the meat or fish — for approximately 20 minutes.
Separately blend the onion, dawadawa, calabash nut and dried herring.
Add a cup of boiling water to the blended mixture.
Wait 5 minutes before adding the ayoyo leaves.
Blend it, or keep stirring with a dedicated cooking broom (ijabe), and let it simmer approximately 10 minutes.
// Optional: use bitter salt to soften the leaves before stirring.
Serve with tuo zaafi (GHA044) and the stew.
chefTips: Wash before cutting. The source is explicit that otherwise the sliminess will not be activated, and the slipperiness is the entire reason for the soup.
Wait five minutes after the boiling water goes into the blended seasoning, before the leaves. That pause lets the dawadawa and herring open up.
An ijabe is the Ghanaian cooking broom, the same tool used for ewedu in Nigeria. It produces a different texture from a blender — stringier and more suspended.
Bitter salt is offered as an optional softener for the leaves. That is an alkali, and like all alkalis it should be used sparingly.
A calabash nut — African nutmeg — is the aromatic here, and fifteen grams of dawadawa is the savoury base. Both are northern markers.
Three hundred and fifty millilitres of palm oil is a great deal for five servings, and it is printed as such. Reduce it if you want, knowing you are departing from the source.
This version is written for an electric pressure cooker, which is why the timings are short. On a stove, give the stew base longer.
commonMistakes: Cutting the leaves before washing them, which kills the slipperiness.
Adding the leaves straight after the water.
Over-boiling, which breaks the mucilage down.
Heavy-handed use of the bitter salt.
Treating the pressure-cooker timings as stove timings.
sources: Adapted from "Hajia's Irresistable Tuo Zaafi with Ayoyo", afrifoodlinks.org. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'By Steyn Hoogakker / Coordinated by ICLEI Africa', dateline 'Accra, Ghana'. No date. Yield as printed: 'Serves 4-6'. The title's misspelling 'Irresistable' is as printed. A NOTE ON THE DOMAIN: this is afrifoodlinks.org, which is NOT the banned afrifoodnetwork.com — the two were checked and are different sites. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 250g beef chunks or 200g fresh local salmon or mushrooms; 150g ayoyo leaves; 15g dawadawa; 1 calabash nut; 50g dried local herring; 1 tbsp salt; 50g hot green pepper; 350ml palm oil; 3 onions; 3 tomatoes; 1 tin tomatoes; 5 cloves of garlic; 20g ginger; 400g corn flour; 150g cassava flour; 1.5L water; 1 seasoning cube dissolved in 250ml water (or 250ml meat stock).
THE KEY INSTRUCTION, verbatim and the most valuable line in the entire northern Ghanaian record: 'Wash the ayoyo leaves before cutting, otherwise the "sliminess" will not be activated'.

Method quoted: stew 'Cook for approximately 20 minutes.' Ayoyo: blend onion, dawadawa, calabash nut and herring; 'Add a cup of boiling water, then wait for 5 minutes before adding the ayoyo leaves. Blend it or keep stirring with a dedicated cooking broom (ijabe) and let it simmer for approximately 10 minutes.' 'You can also use bitter salt for softening the leaves, before stirring.' TZ: 'Add the water (1150 ml) and bring to the boil. Combine the cassava and corn flour, and slowly add it to the EPC, stirring to mix well. When it has thickened, partially cover the pot with the lid, then wait 10 minutes for the tuo zaafi to be ready.'

A QUANTITY THAT DOES NOT RECONCILE, flagged and NOT corrected: the ingredient list says '1.5L water' but the method states 1150 ml plus a cup. The two do not add up. It is printed that way and both figures are recorded.

AN ADAPTATION CAVEAT: this is an ELECTRIC PRESSURE COOKER version, which is why its cooking times are shorter than a stove-top method would need. The author's own note is worth having: 'try to use indigenous ingredients... use millet dough or flour instead of corn or cassava flour.' So the author himself flags corn and cassava flour as the less indigenous choice.

WHAT AYOYO IS, from the GAIN 2016 focused ethnographic study of Karaga District, Northern Region — authors as printed Margaret Armar-Klemesu, Sawudatu Zakariah-Akoto and Sarah Osei-Menya for the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, November 2016. Verbatim: 'Ayoyo soup is a very slimy soup prepared similar to light soup but with added ayoyo leaves which are very slimy in nature.' And on the pairing: 'TZ: Hot thick porridge made from whole grain maize flour and consumed with vegetable soup (Usually green leafy vegetables (ayoyo/bra) with dried okro or groundnut paste or pounded raw groundnuts)'. It lists dawadawa as 'fermented locust bean paste' used as seasoning.

THE BOTANY, from Whitby 1968: 'Jute leaves (Corchorus sp), leaves of False Sesame (Ceratotheca sesamoides); all are mucilaginous.' On northern leaf soups generally: 'These soups may include groundnut paste or dawadawa (fermented locust bean) or kantong (other fermented oil seeds).' Note kantong as a further fermented oilseed condiment, which no other source consulted describes.
A SOURCE REJECTED: a Pulse Ghana 'Ayoyo soup with beef stew' page had no byline, no date and no quantities.
THE LEAF-HANDLING DISAGREEMENT across sources is set out in the sources at GHA073 and is not repeated here.

ON DAWADAWA QUANTITIES, and the fact that nobody justifies them: 15 g here; 2 tablespoons in Adwoa Fofie's ayoyo (GHA073); 2 tablespoons of locust beans in the bito soup (GHA075); 1 teaspoon in a flagged source. NOWHERE IS A RATIO JUSTIFIED by any source.
reheating: Gentle heat. Do not boil, or the slipperiness is lost.
healthBenefits: Jute leaf is exceptionally high in vitamins A, C and E, calcium, iron and folate.
The mucilage is a soluble fibre with documented cholesterol-binding activity.
Dawadawa supplies B vitamins and plant protein.
Dried herring adds calcium, iodine and omega-3 fats.
culturalNote: Ayoyo is to northern Ghana what ewedu is to western Nigeria — the same jute leaf, the same prized slipperiness, even the same broom used to stir it. That the instruction to wash before cutting appears in only one documented source is the kind of knowledge that usually passes from hand to hand and never gets written down.
